newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS-Cocoa, coffee underpinned by covering.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS-Cocoa, coffee underpinned by covering.

text.p: A host of short covering deals seem to the only talking point of otherwise quiet coffee and cocoa options markets this week.
Coffee traders, taking the view that the market's latest bounce may extend further but will eventually be exhausted, were seen covering shorts on January and March calls.
But they seemed to avoid engaging in outright purchases, reflecting the overall downtrend in futures prices.
"You pick the premium thinking the market may have a bit more corrective bounce. You don't want your call to be triggered," said one coffee options market maker.

In business-starved cocoa the inclination was to protect the downside risk, covering March puts as futures headed lower. These were merely directional players who bought calls above the market and sold puts below, feeling the market would go up.

Traders said cocoa futures seemed to be trapped between 900 and 950 stg basis March and a strategy best suited to such lethargic conditions was to play on the time decay of options by selling 975 calls and 900 puts.
In coffee, the most active calls were January $1,400 and $1,350 which seemed most at risk to be triggered with less than a week before the expiry. The premium on these was around $7-8.

Coffee futures motored higher earlier this week in a technical reaction to an oversold condition and on New York gains after positive stock news. But upside movements were seen capped with origins lurking above the market.
Roaster interest remained flimsy and production of robusta coffee was heading into a seasonal upswing, traders said.
Options traders said the January position expiring on December 18 could stir up some delta hedging if futures values edged closer to $1,400 which is the strike which houses most of the open interest.
"It's a long way to $1,400 but you never know," said one.
Some short covering on out-of-the-money March calls were also cited with interest clustered around $1,500. Business also featured sales of outright puts at $1,250 and $1,200.
"If the market seems a bit toppy off the bounce, you can pick up cheap puts or put spreads for $1,200, $1,150. These shouldn't be expensive," recommended the market maker.

Coffee volatilies firmed a few points -- more so on the March contract which had previously been under pressure. Prices were skewed toward calls with out-of-the-money March calls trading at volatilities of around 28-30 percent.

Cocoa volatilities meanwhile picked up on the puts as players covered shorts around the March 950 stg. Implied volatilities were around 15-17 percent for the puts and between 18-21 for out-of-the-money calls.
Cocoa futures have recently backed away from attempts to challenge higher levels, taking refuge in cosy ranges while awaiting new data from the Ivory Coast to gauge the size of the crop.
Estimates so far have a wide range as analysts are trying to establish whether last year's record crop in West Africa was a fluke or the beginning of a new trend.
Industry demand has been hesitant at best while origins are ready to sell into any rally while shipments are approaching seasonal peaks.
